Case study · Invia Flights · 2025 to 2026

Three moments that decide a flight booking

Three features for an online travel agency, each answering a customer's doubt at the moment it appears. KPI-driven: every feature fed the north star, and A/B tests validated each iteration.

Role
UX/UI Designer, owner of these three features end to end
Product
Invia Flights: fluege.de and other flight booking brands
Platforms
Web, iOS, Android
Method
KPI-driven product design: UX KPIs and guardrails, A/B tests, session recordings
Proof
All three features are live in the booking funnel on fluege.de (opens in a new tab).

Challenge

Customers compare the same flight on every portal, so trust decides where they book. The old offer card pushed them toward the member price, and Trustpilot reviews and funnel drop-offs showed they felt it. Three doubts cost us bookings at three points of the funnel: in the search results, during booking and at payment.

Impact

  • ConversionAcross the booking funnel measured
  • 3Features shipped, one redesigned and two new, each layout A/B tested
  • LiveAll three features, still in the funnel today
  • Web, iOS, AndroidOne pattern across all platforms

Collaboration

I owned the design process for the three features end to end, from UX KPIs to the final UI. I worked closely with the product owner, who owned the product decisions, and with the web and mobile developers who built the features. Before designing, the product owner and I agreed on the north star, the UX KPIs and the guardrails that would measure success or failure.

Context

Customers compare the same flight everywhere. Trust decides where they book.

Invia Flights is one of the largest online travel agencies in the German market, with brands like fluege.de and airline-direct.de on web, iOS and Android.

I owned three features at three points of the funnel. Each one answers a question that used to cost us bookings.

  1. 1 · Search results Offer Box "Is this the best offer, and is the member price worth it?"
  2. 2 · Booking Flex Ticket "What if my plans change?"
  3. 3 · Payment Price Guarantee "What if the price drops after I book?"

What made it hard

Every feature needed UX KPIs that fed the north star

We worked KPI-driven. Conversion was our north star, and with flights plus add-ons like the Flex Ticket, the whole basket counted. For every feature I defined UX KPIs that feed it, plus guardrails that must not drop. The KPIs decided whether a feature succeeded or failed. A/B tests validated each iteration on the way.

That made trade-offs visible early. The member price was a business goal, so anything that made the normal price more visible put member sign-ups at risk: a guardrail, not the goal.

The same features ran on web, iOS and Android, built by different teams. A pattern only counted if it worked on all three.

Decision 1 · Search results · Offer Box

From a push to an honest choice

"Is this the best offer, and is the member price worth it?"

Problem. The old card had one big button that selected the member price. The normal price hid in a small text link. Customers saw a single price and only found out later in the booking funnel that it came with a paid membership, unusual for the market. Trustpilot reviews and drop-offs later in the funnel, analyzed in session recordings and analytics, showed the cost: customers felt pushed.

Tension. The membership was one of the main revenue streams the business wanted to grow, so the product owner was cautious about showing the normal price. But selling flights mattered more. We agreed that conversion on flights counts in the end, with member clicks as the guardrail. Our first job as the UX team: make customers want the offer and be willing to start a deal. The UX KPI was getting people into the booking funnel.

Hypothesis. If both prices carry equal weight, customers feel less pushed and book more, even if fewer pick the member price.

My approach

The Offer Box is the first touchpoint where customers decide whether they want to book at all. So it had to be a modular system we could test quickly and iteratively. I turned the card into an honest choice, with two equal price buttons side by side, and built it from slots, so new features and layouts can be tested one slot at a time without a redesign. The chip slot was planned from the start for features still to come, like the Flex Ticket in the next chapter. Each version was A/B tested against the previous card and checked in session recordings.

Modular component

One box, four slots: top, itinerary, price actions and footer. Each slot changes on its own, so new features were added without a redesign and button layouts could be A/B tested. The tour plays one round, then it's your turn.

Result

A clear conversion uplift in the A/B test measured, despite fewer upsell clicks. A less pushy offer sold more flights, and it is still live today. The test also surfaced ideas for the next round, ready to be tested in their own slots.

Decision 2 · Booking · Flex Ticket

From stacked tickets to a side-by-side comparison

"What if my plans change?"

A flexible ticket lets customers cancel shortly before departure and get most of the price back. We A/B tested two layouts, iterated on the winner, then adapted it for the apps. Thanks to the chip slot in the Offer Box, the Flex Ticket also shows up right in the search results, without touching the card's design.

Result

Variant B with the hint won the A/B test. Roughly a quarter of customers chose the Flex Ticket range, and conversion rose. People booked who would otherwise have waited.

We also aligned design system decisions with the mobile development team. Web and apps now feel more consistent, and both teams avoid duplicate work.

Decision 3 · Payment · Price Guarantee

From early in the funnel to the payment step

"What if the price drops after I book?"

If the fare drops after booking, customers get part of the saving back as a voucher. We tested where in the funnel the offer belongs, then made the mechanics easy to understand.

Result

About three in four customers kept the Price Guarantee range.

What I took away

Agreeing on the metric settled the biggest conflict

The Product Owner worried about member sign-ups. Agreeing on conversion as the north star and member clicks as the guardrail settled it before the first sketch. The chip slot, planned in the Offer Box from the start, later let the Flex Ticket show up in search results without a redesign.

What I would do differently

Today the Price Guarantee ships pre-selected. I would make it an active choice: a guarantee customers pick themselves builds more trust, and trust is what all three features are about.

The variants that lost taught me the most. Happy to walk you through them.
